title: Vocabulary Building — The Deep Dive

pts: Depth of knowledge includes collocation, register, connotation and typical grammatical patterns — not just a translation.
A learner with deep knowledge of 2,000 words often communicates better than one with shallow knowledge of 8,000.
Vocabulary tests that check only meaning miss most of what 'knowing' a word requires.

v: Board; a web template per group

items: Write one familiar word in the centre of the board: heavy.
Ask: ‘What do we know about this word?’ Build a web together with branches for sound, spelling, meaning(s), words that go with it, opposite, formal or informal, grammar.
Groups receive a new word (rain, decide, market, careful) and build their own web.
Groups present one branch that surprised them.
Learners add one web per week to their vocabulary notebook for a word they want to ‘own’.
Make it a race: which group can fill the most branches correctly in five minutes?
Build a web in two languages: the home-language word next to the English word, and compare the branches.
Support: provide branch labels with one example already filled.
Stretch: add a branch for ‘other meanings’ (heavy rain, heavy traffic, a heavy heart).

lines: Sound: /ˈhevi/, stress on the first syllable
Meanings: weighs a lot; very strong or intense (heavy rain); serious or sad (a heavy heart)
Goes with: rain, traffic, bag, smoker, meal
Opposite: light
Grammar: adjective; heavier, heaviest
Register: neutral

blocks.x: Depth versus breadth: a learner who knows 2,000 words well can often communicate better than one who knows many more words only by translation.

body: Figure 5.1 What it means to know a word

Purpose: to make word knowledge visible. Content: a spider diagram with a word in the centre (heavy) and seven labelled branches: ‘sound’, ‘spelling’, ‘meanings’, ‘goes with’, ‘opposite’, ‘grammar’, ‘formal or informal?’, each with a small example. Style: organic hand-drawn feel, one accent colour, lots of white space. Board version: as described.

items: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries online or Cambridge Dictionary online (both free). Entries show pronunciation, grammar, collocations and example sentences, which map directly onto the branches of the web.

blocks.x: A good learner’s dictionary shared between groups, or the teacher as ‘dictionary’ for one question per group.

pts: The most frequent 1,000 word families cover roughly 80% of everyday running text.
Time spent on rare words has a poor return compared to consolidating high-frequency ones.
Frequency lists are a syllabus decision tool, not just a vocabulary-app gimmick.

v: Twenty words on cards; a frequency band list (see model language)

items: Give groups twenty word cards. Ask them to sort the words from ‘most common’ to ‘least common’ in English.
Reveal the frequency bands. Discuss surprises.
Ask: ‘If you had only one hour, which ten would you learn?’
Show how learners can check a word’s frequency themselves (see digital tools).
Groups choose five words from their textbook and check their frequency.
Compare learners’ guesses with their own textbook: are the most common words taught first?
With adults, use words from their workplace.
Support: use ten words.
Stretch: learners explain why some rare words are still worth learning (a word crucial for their job or exam).

blocks.x: Illustrative frequency bands (confirm with a current list before classroom use):

lines: Very common (first 1,000 word families): make, time, people, because, good, house
Common (second 1,000): decide, weather, careful, market, prepare
Less common: heritage, reluctant, commute, irrigate

blocks.x: On coverage: the most frequent 1,000 word families account for a large majority, roughly three-quarters or more, of the running words in typical written texts, and a larger share of speech (Nation 2006). [VERIFY exact percentages against the tables in Nation 2006 before stating a single figure.]

body: Purpose: to show how unevenly words are used. Content: a curve falling steeply from left to right. The left side, labelled ‘the first 1,000 word families’, is shaded dark and covers most of the area under the curve. Further bands are shaded progressively lighter, with a long thin tail labelled ‘thousands of rare words’. Axis labels: ‘word families, most to least common’ and ‘how often they appear’. Style: clean data-style illustration, no exact figures unless verified. Board version: a steep curve with the left part shaded.

items: English Vocabulary Profile (Cambridge; free online, registration may be required). Shows the CEFR level at which each meaning of a word is typically known by learners.
Compleat Lexical Tutor – VocabProfile (free, lextutor.ca). Paste a text to see which words fall into which frequency bands.

blocks.x: Use a printed high-frequency word list and highlight words already taught in the textbook in one colour and words not yet taught in another.

pts: Collocations and multi-word expressions ('take a chance', 'in the long run') are stored and retrieved as single units.
Teaching single words and expecting natural combination later under-prepares learners for fluent speech.
Chunking reduces processing load in real-time conversation, which is where fluency actually breaks down.

v: A short dialogue with chunks highlighted; chunk cards

items: Learners listen to and read a short dialogue (see model language).
They underline every group of words that ‘comes together’: by the way, see you later, I’m not sure.
Check together. Explain that fluent speakers store these as single units.
Give each pair a set of chunk cards. They write a new short dialogue using at least five chunks.
Pairs perform their dialogues. The class listens and ticks chunks on a list.
‘Chunk bingo’: learners tick chunks as they hear them in a teacher-read story.
Learners collect chunks from films or cricket commentary in a notebook.
Support: provide a gapped dialogue with chunks to insert.
Stretch: learners use chunks in a two-minute unscripted conversation.

lines: A: Hi! Long time no see. How are things?
B: Not bad, thanks. I’ve been really busy with exams.
A: Oh, I see. By the way, are you free this weekend?
B: I’m not sure. It depends on the weather.
A: No problem. Let me know later.
Collocations: heavy rain, make a decision
Fixed phrases: by the way, of course
Sentence frames: Would you mind if I…?, It depends on…

body: Purpose: to contrast single-word and chunk storage. Content: on the left, a messy pile of single word tiles (by, the, way, of, course). On the right, neat blocks each holding a whole chunk (by the way, of course, It depends on…), stacked like building bricks. Style: playful, three-dimensional tiles. Board version: single words in a scatter, chunks in boxes.

items: SkELL (free). Search a word to see its most frequent collocations in real English, useful for deciding which chunks to teach.

blocks.x: A class ‘chunk wall’ organized by function: greeting, agreeing, asking for help, changing the topic.

pts: Extensive reading builds vocabulary incidentally through repeated exposure in context.
High-value but lower-frequency items usually need explicit teaching — incidental exposure alone is too slow.
Use explicit teaching to accelerate what incidental learning would eventually deliver anyway.

v: A short reading text (250 words); five pre-selected key words

items: Explicit. Pre-teach five words that are essential to the text and unlikely to be guessed. Use pictures, examples and a quick check.
Incidental. Learners read the text for meaning, with a gist task. Do not stop to explain other new words.
After reading, ask learners to find three words they didn’t know but could still understand.
Discuss how they understood them (context, similarity to another word, picture).
Learners add the five pre-taught words and one self-found word to their notebooks with an example sentence.
Use a graded reader chapter from the class library (Unit 3).
Give half the class the pre-taught words and half not; compare understanding.
Support: provide a short glossary for the text beyond the five words.
Stretch: learners identify which new words are high frequency and worth learning.

blocks.x: Choosing words to pre-teach: ask two questions of each unknown word in a text.

lines: Is it essential for understanding the main idea? If yes, consider pre-teaching.
Can it be guessed from context? If yes, leave it for learners to work out.

body: Purpose: to show explicit and incidental learning working together. Content: two paths leading to the same small house labelled ‘known word’. One path is short and straight, labelled ‘explicit: taught directly’. The other is longer and winding through a landscape of books, labelled ‘incidental: met many times in reading and listening’. Style: storybook illustration, soft colours. Board version: two lines leading to a box.

items: StoryWeaver (free). Choose a story at the right level for incidental learning; print or project it.

blocks.x: Any short, interesting text: a newspaper paragraph, a story from a previous year’s textbook, a short biography.

body: English has absorbed many words from Indian languages over several centuries. Bungalow, shampoo, jungle, pyjamas and loot all came into English from Indian languages. A quick class investigation into the origins of everyday English words often surprises learners and shows that the traffic between English and their own languages runs both ways.

pts: New vocabulary needs an estimated 6–8+ spaced encounters before it moves into durable memory.
Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows the sharpest drop-off happens within the first day after learning.
A single presentation-and-forget lesson structure works against how memory actually consolidates.
points.who: Hermann Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve; spaced-repetition research

v: 10 minutes set-up, then 5 minutes several times a week
Small cards; a shoebox or envelope divided into five sections

items: Learners make word cards: the English word or chunk on one side, a picture or translation on the other.
All new cards go into section 1.
Every day (or every lesson), learners test themselves on section 1. Cards they remember move to section 2; cards they forget stay in section 1.
Section 2 is tested every few days, section 3 weekly, section 4 every two weeks, section 5 monthly. Any forgotten card goes back to section 1.
Once a month, learners count how many cards have reached section 5.
Use a class box for shared vocabulary.
Pair learners to test each other rather than themselves.
Support: start with three sections instead of five.
Stretch: write an example sentence on the back instead of a translation.

blocks.x: A simple review schedule after a new word is taught:

lines: Same day → next lesson → after about a week → after about two weeks → after about a month

blocks.x: How many encounters? Estimates vary widely with the word, the learner and the task. Research on incidental learning suggests anything from around six to more than twenty encounters may be needed for a word to be reliably remembered (Webb 2007; Uchihara, Webb and Yanagisawa 2019). The practical message is the same: plan for repeated meetings, not a single presentation.

body: Figure 5.5 The forgetting curve and spaced review

Purpose: to show why spacing works. Content: a graph with ‘time’ on the horizontal axis and ‘how much is remembered’ on the vertical. A steep grey curve falls quickly after the first lesson (labelled ‘no review’). A second, coloured line falls, then jumps up at each review point (labelled ‘review 1’, ‘review 2’, ‘review 3’) and falls more slowly each time. Style: clear, simple chart without exact numbers. Board version: two curves drawn by hand.

items: Anki (free on desktop and Android; paid on iOS). A digital flashcard system that schedules reviews automatically based on how well each card is remembered.
Quizlet (free basic version). The ‘Learn’ mode repeats items learners get wrong more often.

blocks.x: The Leitner box described in the activity, made from a shoebox and card dividers. It is the paper ancestor of most digital flashcard apps.

pts: Teaching prefixes, suffixes and word families lets learners unlock related words from one root.
Knowing '-tion' forms a noun from a verb, for instance, extends vocabulary faster than memorising items one by one.
This is especially efficient for academic and Latinate vocabulary in EAP contexts.

v: Board; a list of prefixes and suffixes

items: Write employ at the base of a tree on the board.
Ask learners to suggest related words. Add branches: employer, employee, employment, unemployed, unemployment.
Circle the added parts and ask what each one does (-er a person who does it; -ee a person it is done to; -ment a noun; un- not).
Groups build trees for new roots: act, happy, use, care.
Groups swap trees and check them with a dictionary.
Play ‘suffix dominoes’: match roots and endings.
With academic learners, focus on -tion, -ity, -ize, -al.
Support: provide the endings; learners attach them.
Stretch: learners find words where the stress moves when a suffix is added (ACT → acTIvity).

blocks.x: Common affixes and what they do:

lines: -tion / -sion: makes a noun (decide → decision)
-ful / -less: full of / without (careful, careless)
un- / dis-: not (unhappy, disagree)
-able: can be done (readable, washable)

blocks.x: Indian English has coined its own words with English word-formation patterns, such as prepone (to move to an earlier time, formed on the model of postpone). Discuss with learners how new words enter a language and where each is used.

body: Purpose: to show how one root grows into many words. Content: a tree with the root word employ on the trunk. Branches carry employer, employee, employment, unemployed, unemployment. Each affix is in a different colour from the root. Small leaves carry labels explaining what each affix does. Style: friendly illustration, legible words. Board version: a trunk and branches in chalk.

items: Wordwall (free basic version). Create a ‘Match up’ or ‘Group sort’ activity pairing roots and affixes.

blocks.x: Root and affix cards cut from paper; learners build words physically on their desks.

pts: Teach learners to infer meaning from surrounding context as a genuine reading strategy.
Flag the risk explicitly: false friends and misleading context can produce confident, wrong guesses.
Follow up guessed meanings with a dictionary check for high-value words worth getting exactly right.

v: Sentences with an invented word; a short text with real unknown words; dictionaries

items: Give sentences with an invented word: The farmer put the grain in the glarb to keep the rats out. Learners guess what glarb means and say how they know.
Teach a simple guessing routine (see model language).
Learners apply the routine to five real unknown words in a short text.
They check their guesses in a dictionary and mark each guess ✓ or ✗.
Discuss the ✗ guesses: why did the context mislead?
Learners write their own ‘glarb’ sentences for others to guess.
Compare guessing in English with guessing in a home language: do the same clues work?
Support: underline the clue words in the sentence.
Stretch: include deceptively transparent words (see model language).

lines: 1. What kind of word is it (noun, verb, adjective)?
2. What do the words around it tell me?
3. Do I recognize any part of it?
4. Does my guess make sense in the sentence? Check if it matters.

blocks.x: Deceptive words look easy to guess but are not (Laufer 1989):

lines: nevertheless is not ‘never the less’; shortcoming is not ‘arriving early’; outline is not ‘a line outside’.

body: Purpose: to show the clues around a word. Content: a sentence in large type with the unknown word in a highlighted box in the middle. Arrows from surrounding words point to the box with small labels: ‘grammar clue’ (the), ‘topic clue’ (grain, rats), ‘word-part clue’. A small warning sign in the corner reads ‘Check if it matters!’ Style: clean, instructional. Board version: sentence with arrows.

items: Cambridge Dictionary online (free). Useful for the checking stage; learners can also see example sentences that confirm or correct their guess.

blocks.x: Paper dictionaries shared between pairs, or the teacher confirms guesses at the end.

body: Give learners a short text with ten unknown words and ask them to guess each one before checking. Count how many guesses were right. Most classes are surprised by both results: guessing works more often than they expected, and fails more often than they would like. That is exactly the balance learners need to understand.

pts: Plan deliberate re-exposure of target vocabulary across future lessons, not just recall drills on the same day.
Interleave old and new vocabulary in tasks so recycling feels purposeful, not like a repeated test.
A word not recycled within a few weeks is, for most learners, effectively not taught.

v: 10 minutes at the start of every third lesson
A list of words taught in the last month

items: Keep a running list of all words and chunks taught, with dates.
Every third lesson, open with a five-minute ‘Mix it’ quiz: five old items and five new ones, in random order.
Use varied formats: definition to word, picture to word, gap-fill, collocation match.
Learners mark their own quizzes and move any forgotten words back to section 1 of their word box (point 5).
Once a term, build a lesson task (a story, a role-play) that requires learners to use at least ten recycled words.
Learners write the quiz for each other.
Use a ‘word auction’: pairs bid points on sentences that use recycled words correctly.
Support: include pictures for older words.
Stretch: learners must use the words in sentences, not just recognize them.

blocks.x: A recycling plan across a unit of four weeks:

lines: Week 1: teach 20 words; recycle 5 in the next lesson.
Week 2: teach 20 new words; mix 10 from week 1 into tasks.
Week 3: new words plus a story task using 10 from weeks 1–2.
Week 4: review quiz on all words; learners choose their ‘top 10 to keep’.

body: Purpose: a planning sheet for teachers. Content: a four-week calendar grid. New words are marked with a star on the day they are taught; circles on later days show planned review points for those words, connected by thin lines. The pattern shows reviews spreading out over time. Style: clean planner layout, two colours. Board version: not applicable.

items: Wordwall or Kahoot! (free basic versions). Quick quiz games for the ‘Mix it’ routine; Kahoot! needs a device per team, Wordwall can be played on one projected screen.

blocks.x: A paper quiz on the board, with answers written by learners in notebooks and marked by a partner.

dek: Unit 5 of 100: why frequency, chunking and spaced recycling matter more than word counts — and how to move vocabulary from recognition into real, retrievable use.

aims.x: This unit explores how vocabulary is actually learned and remembered, and what that means for teaching. It argues for knowing fewer words more deeply, choosing words by frequency, teaching chunks rather than single words, and planning for repeated, spaced encounters.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe what it means to ‘know’ a word, beyond its translation;
use frequency information to decide which words to teach;
teach and recycle lexical chunks and collocations;
balance incidental learning through reading with explicit teaching;
plan spaced review in line with what is known about forgetting;
teach word formation to multiply learners’ vocabulary;
teach guessing from context as a strategy with clear limits;
build systematic recycling into a scheme of work.

why: Why this matters. A learner can 'know' thousands of words on a list and still fail to retrieve the right one in real time. Depth and recycling close that gap — breadth alone doesn't.

background.x: Ask a learner how many English words they know and they will often point to a vocabulary notebook: a list of English words with translations. It is an understandable picture, and a misleading one. Knowing a word involves knowing how it sounds and is spelled, what it means and in how many senses, which words it usually keeps company with, how formal it is, and how it behaves grammatically. Paul Nation (2013) lists these aspects of word knowledge in detail. A translation covers only one of them.

Two further facts shape vocabulary teaching. The first is that English words are very unevenly used. A small number of very common words make up most of the words in any ordinary text, and the rest appear rarely. Choosing which words to teach first is therefore one of the most consequential decisions a teacher makes. The second is that memory decays quickly. A word met once in a lesson is, for most learners, a word soon lost unless it is met again, and met again at the right intervals.

Indian classrooms bring particular strengths to vocabulary work. Learners who already manage two or three languages are experienced at noticing that words do not map neatly from one language to another. English itself carries many words from Indian languages, and Indian English has contributed words and usages of its own. These connections make excellent starting points for talking about how words live and travel.

items: Word web check. Give learners a word taught three weeks earlier and ask them to complete as many branches of the web as they can.
Frequency awareness. Ask learners to choose which five of ten words they would learn first and explain why.
Chunk production. In a short speaking task, count the number of taught chunks each learner uses without prompting.
Retention over time. Test the same set of words one week and one month after teaching; compare results and adjust the recycling plan.
How do your learners record new vocabulary? What do their notebooks tell you about what they think ‘knowing a word’ means?
How do you decide which words to teach? Would frequency information change your choices?
How many times will a word taught today be met again in your lessons this month?
Do you teach words singly or in chunks? What is one chunk you could teach tomorrow instead of a single word?
How do you use your learners’ other languages when teaching vocabulary?

terms.def: A meaningful element attached to a word stem to form a new word or word form, such as the prefix un- in unhappy or the suffix -ness in kindness; teaching common affixes helps learners work out new words.
The number of words a learner knows at least at a basic level of form and meaning; contrast depth of vocabulary knowledge.
A combination of words that frequently occur together, such as make a decision or heavy rain; learners who know collocations sound more natural and fluent.
The quality of words that look as if their meaning can be worked out from their parts but cannot, such as outline (not ‘out’ + ‘line’) (Laufer 1989).
How well a learner knows a word, including its forms, meanings, collocations, register and use in context; contrast breadth of vocabulary knowledge.
Learning in which the learner is aware of what is being learned, often with conscious attention to rules or forms, such as studying a grammar rule or a word list. It contrasts with implicit learning.
The pattern by which memory of newly learned material drops quickly and then more slowly over time unless it is reviewed (Ebbinghaus 1885). It is the basis for spaced review of vocabulary.
A group of words ranked by frequency, such as the most common 1,000 or 2,000 words. Knowing a learner’s frequency band helps teachers choose readable texts and target vocabulary.
Working out the meaning of an unknown word from clues in the surrounding text, such as examples, contrasts or word parts. It is a key strategy for extensive reading.
Learning that happens without deliberate intention, as a by-product of doing something else, such as picking up words while reading a story for pleasure.

A spaced-repetition method, devised by Sebastian Leitner, in which flashcards move between boxes: a card answered correctly moves to a box reviewed less often, and a card answered wrongly goes back to the first box.
A multi-word unit stored and used as a whole, such as by the way or I’d like to; the lexical approach treats such chunks as central to fluency (Lewis 1993).
An affix added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning, such as un- in unhappy or re- in rewrite.

Planned reintroduction of previously taught language in new contexts and activities so that it is met, retrieved and used repeatedly over time. Recycling helps vocabulary and grammar move from recognition towards fluent, confident use.
Reviewing items, especially vocabulary, at gradually increasing intervals, just as they are about to be forgotten. Many flashcard apps schedule reviews automatically using this principle.
A morpheme added to the end of a word to change its meaning or word class, such as -ness in kindness or -ful in helpful. Teaching common suffixes helps learners work out and build word families.
The percentage of running words in a text that a reader knows. Research suggests about 98 per cent coverage is needed for comfortable unassisted reading (Hu and Nation 2000).
A base word together with its inflected and derived forms, such as help, helps, helped, helpful and helpless (Bauer and Nation 1993). Word families are often used to count vocabulary size.
All that is involved in knowing a word, including its form, meaning, grammar, collocations, register and use (Nation 2013). Knowing a word is gradual and multidimensional, not all-or-nothing.
